title: Exposure effects in the classroom: The development of affinity among students
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; title and indexed keywords (mere exposure effect, familiarity, attractiveness, classroom interaction) indicate a classroom field study of how repeated mere presence in a lecture builds affinity among students.
why_for_us: Mere repeated presence in the same room can build liking without talk: let Kuba simply keep turning up at the same training sessions or the registry desk before anything is said.

title: Is actual similarity necessary for attraction? A meta-analysis of actual and perceived similarity
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
finding: Meta-analysis of 460 effect sizes from 313 studies: attraction correlated with actual similarity r = .47 and perceived similarity r = .39 (per authors). Actual similarity mattered in no- and short-interaction studies but was not significant in existing relationships, while perceived similarity predicted attraction across all contexts.
why_for_us: What matters is the moment one of them notices 'we think alike' (both hate the same sloppy deed draft), not a checklist of shared traits; make the similarity perceived on screen.

title: A Two-Dimensional Model for the Study of Interpersonal Attraction
finding: Theoretical review proposing that attraction follows from evaluations of a target's capacity to facilitate the perceiver's goals and the target's willingness to do so (per authors).
why_for_us: Competence (Kuba knows the land-register procedure) is not enough; a beat where he actually uses it to help Zosia's overworked aunt signals willingness, the second ingredient.

title: The effect of a pratfall on increasing interpersonal attractiveness
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; the classic Aronson, Willerman and Floyd experiment whose title reports that a blunder (pratfall) increased the interpersonal attractiveness of the person who committed it; the effect is usually described as applying to a person first seen as competent.
why_for_us: An over-confident Kuba becomes more likeable when a small, visible slip punctures his competence (spilling coffee on a stamp pad), provided he was shown as capable first.

title: Sex differences in mate preferences revisited: Do people know what they initially desire in a romantic partner?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Speed-dating study with longitudinal follow-up: participants stated the usual sex-differentiated ideals (men value looks, women earning prospects), but no sex differences appeared in what predicted actual romantic interest in partners met in person, and pre-event ideal preferences failed to predict desire at the event (per authors).
why_for_us: Zosia can state she would never date a 'climber' like Kuba and still be drawn to him in person; the stated-vs-revealed gap is realistic, not hypocrisy.

title: Is Romantic Desire Predictable? Machine Learning Applied to Initial Romantic Attraction
finding: Two speed-dating studies, 100+ pre-date self-report measures, random forests: models predicted 4-18% of actor variance and 7-27% of partner variance but none of the relationship-specific variance (who desires whom uniquely) (per authors).
why_for_us: Chemistry between these two specific people cannot be explained by their profiles, so the show should earn it through interaction beats, not through exposition about compatible traits.

title: Selective Versus Unselective Romantic Desire: Not All Reciprocity Is Created Equal
finding: Speed-dating report using the Social Relations Model: distinguishes dyadic reciprocity (liking shared uniquely between two people) from generalized reciprocity, and frames the question of whether being liked increases romantic liking versus the 'hard to get' hypothesis (per authors; results not in the OpenAlex abstract, which is truncated).
why_for_us: Interest that is clearly specific to Zosia (he is not this attentive with everyone) is the kind of reciprocity that attracts; generic charm toward all apprentices would undercut him.

title: Perceived, not actual, similarity predicts initial attraction in a live romantic context: Evidence from the speed‐dating paradigm
finding: Speed-dating study (about 12 four-minute dates per participant): perceived but not actual similarity significantly predicted romantic liking, and perceived similarity was a much weaker predictor when measured on specific traits rather than generally (per authors).
why_for_us: A shared glance of 'same thought' after a client's absurd request does more than revealing they both like the same band; play the felt sense of being alike.

title: Some evidence for heightened sexual attraction under conditions of high anxiety.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Field experiment: male passersby approached by an attractive female interviewer on a fear-arousing suspension bridge wrote more sexual content in TAT stories and more often attempted post-experiment contact than men on a non-fear-arousing bridge, while a comparison condition showed no bridge differences (per authors; abstract truncated). A single 1974 field study with small samples by modern standards.
why_for_us: Sharing a stressful moment (a rushed signing, a furious client) can be the moment attraction flickers; stage their closest beat right after a shared adrenaline spike.

title: Arousal and attraction: Evidence for automatic and controlled processes.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Meta-analysis of arousal-manipulating experiments plus a review and an experiment: arousal affected attraction even when its source was relatively unambiguous, but the effect was stronger when the source was ambiguous; cognitive busyness interfered with people's correction for the arousal source (per authors). The abstract gives no k or effect size.
why_for_us: The arousal-attraction transfer works best when the characters are too busy to notice why their hearts race: a hectic deadline day is better than a calm one for a charged glance.

title: “He Loves Me, He Loves Me Not . . . ”: Uncertainty Can Increase Romantic Attraction
finding: Experiment: college women saw Facebook profiles of men told to (a) like them a lot, (b) like them an average amount, or (c) either (uncertain). Women were more attracted to men who liked them a lot than average, but most attracted in the uncertain condition, and this was explained by thinking about the men more (per authors). Single small-sample study, women only.
why_for_us: Leave Zosia unsure whether Kuba's favour was meant for her or was routine politeness; the not-knowing that keeps her thinking about him is the engine, so do not resolve it within the episode.

title: When does playing hard to get increase romantic attraction?
finding: Two studies: playing hard to get increased the other person's wanting but decreased their liking, and only when that person was already psychologically committed to pursuing the relationship; without commitment it decreased both (per authors).
why_for_us: Zosia's walk-outs mid-sentence only intensify Kuba's wanting because he is already invested after nine months; early in the series the same behaviour would just make him lose interest, and it costs her some of his liking.

title: "Playing hard to get": Understanding an elusive phenomenon.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; the classic Walster et al. series of studies on whether a hard-to-get partner is more desirable, which the later literature summarises as little support for general hard-to-get and support for a selectively hard-to-get partner (easy for me, hard for others).
why_for_us: If Zosia is cool with everyone but slightly warmer with Kuba, that selective availability is the believable version of 'hard to get'.

title: Parental interference and romantic love: The Romeo and Juliet effect.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; the original Driscoll, Davis and Lipetz longitudinal survey that coined the 'Romeo and Juliet effect' (parental interference associated with increased romantic love). See RP015 (Sinclair et al. 2014), which failed to replicate it.
why_for_us: Do not rely on the aunt's disapproval to fuel the romance; the original finding is not robust (see replication).

title: Revisiting the Romeo and Juliet Effect (): Reexamining the Links Between Social Network Opinions and Romantic Relationship Outcomes
finding: FAILED REPLICATION: longitudinal replication of Driscoll et al. (1972) with N = 396 followed 3-4 months using original and modern measures found no Romeo and Juliet effect; higher interference or lower approval from friends and family predicted poorer relationship quality on every outcome, also confirmed in a meta-analysis (per authors).
why_for_us: If the aunt or Kuba's colleagues disapprove, that should strain the romance, not inflame it; the believable arc is that Kuba wins the aunt's approval, which unlocks Zosia.

title: Interruption, recall and resumption: a meta-analysis of the Zeigarnik and Ovsiankina effects
finding: Meta-analysis: no memory advantage for unfinished tasks (Zeigarnik effect not supported overall), but a general tendency to resume interrupted tasks (Ovsiankina effect) was found (per authors).
why_for_us: Zosia's interrupted sentences will not make viewers or Kuba remember better, but they do create a pull to come back and finish; write the next episode's first beat as her resuming the exact sentence.

title: Intimacy and Scarcity of Self-Disclosure: Effects on Interpersonal Attraction for Males and Females
finding: Factorial experiment testing whether liking for a person who discloses intimately is mediated by the perceived scarcity of the disclosure (whether the partner would ordinarily reveal such information to others) (per authors; results truncated in the abstract). Same-sex partners.
why_for_us: A personal confession lands harder if it is clear Zosia does not tell this to anyone else ('nikomu tego nie mówiłam'); scarcity, not intimacy alone, carries the weight.

title: Looking and loving: The effects of mutual gaze on feelings of romantic love
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; the Kellerman, Lewis and Laird experiment whose title reports that induced mutual gaze between opposite-sex strangers increased feelings of romantic love (classic small-sample lab study).
why_for_us: With low-expressivity avatars, a held mutual look (2-3 s longer than the dialogue needs) is the cheapest, most legible signal of interest; let one of them break it first.

title: The Ability to Judge the Romantic Interest of Others
finding: Observers watching speed-date videos predicted daters' romantic interest; men and women observers were equally accurate, more accurate for male interest, while predictions of female interest were just above chance; clips as short as 10 s sufficed, and some daters masked their intentions (per authors).
why_for_us: It is realistic that nobody, Kuba included, can read Zosia's interest, while Kuba's is obvious to the aunt and to the audience within seconds.

title: The sexual overperception bias: Evidence of a systematic bias in men from a survey of naturally occurring events
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; Haselton's survey of naturally occurring events whose title reports a systematic male bias to overperceive women's sexual interest.
why_for_us: Kuba reading too much into Zosia's friendliness is a believable comic misread, but the show must let her correct it and him accept it.

title: Sexual overperception: Power, mating motives, and biases in social judgment.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Four experiments: having power over an opposite-sex person activated sexual concepts and increased expectations of sexual interest from a subordinate, but only when the subordinate was romantically available (per authors).
why_for_us: Keep Kuba and Zosia as equals (both apprentices); if he ever supervises her, his reading of her signals becomes biased and the romance turns uncomfortable.

title: Testing Error Management Theory: Exploring the Commitment Skepticism Bias and the Sexual Overperception Bias
finding: Face-to-face stranger interactions with 111 man-woman dyads broadly supported error management theory (men overestimate women's sexual interest; women underestimate men's commitment interest), with possible boundary conditions (per authors).
why_for_us: Zosia's scepticism about whether Kuba is serious is a documented bias, not coldness; his proof has to be consistent behaviour over episodes, not one declaration.

title: Individual Differences in the Communication of Romantic Interest: Development of the Flirting Styles Inventory
finding: Survey (N = 5,020) supporting five flirting styles: traditional, physical, sincere, playful and polite; women scored higher on all styles except playful (per authors).
why_for_us: Give each a distinct style: Kuba playful (teasing, competitive), Zosia polite/sincere (careful, rule-bound, genuine questions); the clash of styles is itself a source of beats.

title: Nonverbal courtship patterns in women
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; Moore's observational field study cataloguing women's nonverbal solicitation behaviours (glances, smiles, hair-flips, postural moves) in social settings.
why_for_us: Women often initiate with small glances that men then 'approach'; a short glance from Zosia before Kuba speaks reverses the cliche of the man as sole initiator.

title: Nonverbal courtship patterns in women: Rejection signaling — An empirical investigation
finding: Observational data from the US producing a typology of women's nonverbal rejection signals, emphasising face, gestures, posture and gaze (per authors; abstract in French).
why_for_us: The show needs clear rejection signals too (turning the torso away, looking at the phone); when Zosia uses them Kuba must back off, which keeps the pursuit respectful.

title: Experimental evidence that women speak in a higher voice pitch to men they find attractive
finding: Experiment measuring women's voice pitch while leaving voicemail messages for masculinised and feminised versions of a male face; the title reports that women spoke in a higher pitch to men they found attractive (per authors; results truncated in the abstract).
why_for_us: A slight pitch rise in Zosia's voice when she answers Kuba (vs. the aunt) is a subtle, audio-only cue that survives limited avatar expressivity; brief the TTS direction accordingly.

title: Physiological synchrony is associated with attraction in a blind date setting
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; blind-date study whose title reports that physiological synchrony (e.g. heart rate, skin conductance) between partners was associated with attraction.
why_for_us: Show synchrony rather than declaring it: both reach for the same file, both sigh at the same moment, matched walking pace in the corridor.

title: Fueled by desire: Sexual activation facilitates the enactment of relationship-initiating behaviors
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
finding: Four studies: in Study 1, participants' desire for an opposite-sex confederate while miming together to music was associated with coded immediacy behaviours (warmth and contact-readiness signals) toward the confederate (per authors; later studies truncated).
why_for_us: Attraction leaks into immediacy: leaning in, facing squarely, closing distance; these body cues are the readable signal when the face cannot do the work.

title: The Experimental Generation of Interpersonal Closeness: A Procedure and Some Preliminary Findings
finding: Lab procedure: over 45 minutes stranger pairs carry out self-disclosure and relationship-building tasks that gradually escalate in intensity; Study 1 found greater post-interaction closeness than comparable small-talk tasks (per authors; further studies truncated in the abstract).
why_for_us: Closeness grows by small escalating steps, not one big confession: across episodes let their questions move from case law to 'why notary?' to 'what are you afraid of?', each one notch deeper.

title: Self-disclosure and liking: A meta-analytic review.
finding: Meta-analysis supporting three disclosure-liking effects: people who make intimate disclosures tend to be liked more, people disclose more to those they like, and people like others as a result of having disclosed to them (per authors; abstract truncated after the first effect, k not shown).
why_for_us: Have Kuba be the one who confides first (e.g. failing an exam once); disclosing makes him likeable and also makes him like Zosia more for having listened.

title: When Does Responsiveness Pique Sexual Interest? Attachment and Sexual Desire in Initial Acquaintanceships
finding: Three studies in which participants discussed a recent negative event with an unfamiliar opposite-sex partner, then rated the partner's responsiveness and their sexual desire; the studies examine when perceived responsiveness raises desire as a function of attachment orientation (per authors; detailed results truncated).
why_for_us: When Zosia vents about her aunt's overload, Kuba's best move is attentive, validating listening, not fixing; responsiveness is attractive, though its effect depends on her attachment style.

title: An Evolutionary Perspective on Humor: Sexual Selection or Interest Indication?
finding: Three studies support an interest-indicator model of humour: both sexes were more likely to initiate humour and to respond to humour from someone they were interested in (per authors; abstract truncated).
why_for_us: Zosia laughing at Kuba's weak joke tells more about her interest than the joke tells about his wit; let her laugh slip out despite herself.

title: My funny valentine: How humor styles affect romantic interest
finding: Vignette experiment (N = 251) comparing affiliative versus aggressive humour styles in relationship initiation on short-term and long-term romantic interest (per authors; results truncated).
why_for_us: Kuba's teasing must stay affiliative (laughing with her at the absurd client) rather than aggressive (laughing at her small office); aggressive humour is the fastest way to lose the audience.

title: Putting laughter in context: Shared laughter as behavioral indicator of relationship well‐being
finding: Spontaneous laughs of 71 heterosexual couples were coded from a video-recorded conversation about how they first met; shared (simultaneous) laughter rather than total laughter was associated with relationship well-being indicators (per authors; abstract truncated).
why_for_us: The moment they both laugh at the same absurd clause is a stronger bond signal than either being funny; recalling 'how we met' at the training is a natural trigger.

title: When Sharing a Laugh Means Sharing More: Testing the Role of Shared Laughter on Short-Term Interpersonal Consequences
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; follow-up whose title reports that shared laughter has short-term interpersonal consequences such as greater perceived similarity and closeness (title only).
why_for_us: One shared laugh can be the hinge of a 60-second episode: before it they spar, after it the tone softens.

title: Gain and loss of esteem as determinants of interpersonal attractiveness
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; the classic Aronson and Linder experiment on the gain-loss effect, in which a confederate whose evaluations of the participant moved from negative to positive is reported to be liked more than one who was positive throughout. Single 1960s lab study; not a romantic context.
why_for_us: The real-psychology basis of 'enemies to lovers': Zosia's earned shift from critical to approving ('no, this time you were right') is worth more to Kuba than constant praise, so her approval must be rare and specific.

title: The repulsion hypothesis: On the nondevelopment of relationships.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; Rosenbaum's paper proposing that the similarity-attraction effect is driven mainly by dissimilarity producing repulsion rather than similarity producing attraction.
why_for_us: Their sparring must be about method, not values: disagreeing on how to draft a clause is fun, disagreeing on honesty with clients would repel.

title: The repulsion hypothesis revisited: Similarity irrelevance or dissimilarity bias?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; Smeaton, Byrne and Murnen's test of Rosenbaum's repulsion hypothesis, which the title frames as similarity irrelevance versus dissimilarity bias (the attraction literature reads it as evidence that similarity also attracts).
why_for_us: Read together with Rosenbaum 1986: both shared ground and avoiding deep value clashes matter; give them a shared core value under the surface argument.

title: Gender differences in implicit self-esteem following a romantic partner’s success or failure.
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Experiments (US and Dutch samples): men's implicit self-esteem was lower when their romantic partner succeeded on a 'social intelligence' task than when she failed, while women's implicit self-esteem was unaffected by partner performance (per authors; later experiments truncated).
why_for_us: When Zosia outshines Kuba in front of the examiner, a flicker of wounded pride is realistic; how he recovers (genuine congratulation) is the character test.

title: (Psychological) Distance Makes the Heart Grow Fonder: Effects of Psychological Distance and Relative Intelligence on Men’s Attraction to Women
finding: Studies of men's attraction to women who outperform them: the authors propose that with a psychologically distant target men prefer a woman who is more intelligent than them, whereas with a psychologically near target (in a live interaction) relative superiority becomes less attractive (per authors; abstract truncated after the hypothesis).
why_for_us: Kuba can admire Zosia's sharpness at a distance (watching her handle a client) yet bristle when she corrects him face to face; that contradiction is psychologically grounded.

title: Is smart sexy? Examining the role of relative intelligence in mate preferences
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; study of whether a partner's intelligence relative to one's own shapes mate preferences (title only).
why_for_us: Competence rivalry between two apprentices is a plausible attraction cue, but check the full text before scripting who prefers whom smarter.

title: Relationship Quality, Commitment, and Stability in Long‐Distance Relationships
finding: Nationally representative sample (N = 870): long-distance relationships reported generally higher relationship quality, more dedication and less felt constraint than close-proximity relationships (per authors; stability results truncated).
why_for_us: Limited contact need not kill the spark; scarce meetings (training sessions, the land-registry queue) can feel more precious, so do not write separation as automatic decline.

title: Time Spent Together and Relationship Quality: Long-Distance Relationships as a Test Case
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
finding: Uses long-distance relationships to test whether time spent together causes satisfaction; notes that experimentally increasing couples' time together did not raise satisfaction in earlier research (per authors; own results truncated).
why_for_us: Zosia's lack of time (the aunt keeps calling) does not have to mean lack of feeling; quality of the brief moments matters more than minutes on screen.

title: Relating at a distance: Negotiating being together and being apart in long-distance relationships
venue: Journal of Social and Personal Relationships
finding: Qualitative couple interviews (20 heterosexual couples) using relational dialectics: partners negotiate contradictions between togetherness and separation, and the transitions between being together and apart are not seamless (per authors).
why_for_us: The transitions themselves (Zosia leaving mid-sentence, coming back later) are where tension lives; script the re-entry moment, not just the exit.

title: Relationship perceptions and persistence: Do fluctuations in perceived partner commitment undermine dating relationships?
venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
finding: Two multiwave longitudinal studies: people whose perceptions of their partner's commitment fluctuated over time were more likely to be in relationships that later ended than people whose perceptions were stable (per authors).
why_for_us: Contrast with RP011 (Whitchurch et al.): uncertainty fuels early attraction, but once something starts, Zosia needs Kuba's commitment to look stable; endless hot-cold would doom them.

title: Perceived versus reported social referent approval and romantic relationship commitment and persistence
finding: Survey of 254 students in relationships plus a male and female friend of each: compares friends' reported opinions with participants' perceptions of network opinions as predictors of commitment and persistence (per authors; results truncated).
why_for_us: What Zosia thinks her aunt thinks of Kuba may matter more than what the aunt actually thinks; a beat where Zosia misreads the aunt's view is credible.

title: His or Her Parents? Perceived Parental Approval of Romantic Relationships Among College Students and Their Partners
venue: Interpersona An International Journal on Personal Relationships
finding: 194 dating couples analysed with the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model: in line with social capital theory, approval from one's own parents (strong ties) and from the partner's parents (weak ties) was linked to lower relationship distress (per authors; abstract truncated). Small open-access journal, few citations.
why_for_us: The aunt functions as Zosia's parent figure; her approval of Kuba is a legitimate milestone in the arc.

title: Disintermediating your friends: How online dating in the United States displaces other ways of meeting
venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
finding: Nationally representative 2017 US survey: for heterosexual couples, meeting online became the most common way to meet, overtaking meeting through friends around 2013, and internet meeting is displacing the roles of family and friends (per authors). US data.
why_for_us: Meeting in person at a professional training is now the less common path, which makes it a small romantic distinction the dialogue can acknowledge ('jak w starych czasach').

title: Aspirational pursuit of mates in online dating markets
finding: Empirical analysis of heterosexual online dating markets in four large US cities, quantifying mate pursuit; the abstract frames dating as a market with competition and desirability hierarchies (per authors; key result that users message partners more desirable than themselves is truncated in the abstract).
why_for_us: Kuba aiming 'above his league' (the sharp, unimpressed Zosia) is typical pursuit behaviour, not arrogance alone.

title: Who's wooing whom II? An experimental investigation of date‐initiation and expectancy violation
finding: Experiment using expectancy violation theory: earlier studies found men read female-initiated first dates in more sexual ways while reporting less intimacy on them; participants evaluated a male or female target after a date initiation (per authors; results truncated). Older US student sample.
why_for_us: If Zosia initiates (asks him for coffee 'about the case'), Kuba may misread it; the misread plus her clarification is a natural, modern beat.

title: When Courtship Persistence Becomes Intrusive Pursuit: Comparing Rejecter and Pursuer Perspectives of Unrequited Attraction
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; Sinclair and Frieze's comparison of how pursuers and rejecters perceive the same unrequited pursuit, as the title states, the point at which courtship persistence becomes intrusive.
why_for_us: Pursuers systematically see their own persistence as milder than targets do; Kuba should back off after a clear 'no', and the show can let him misjudge once and correct.

title: Why Doesn’t He Just Leave Me Alone? Persistent Pursuit: A Critical Review of Theories and Evidence
finding: OpenAlex record has no abstract; critical review of theories and evidence on persistent pursuit after rejection (title only).
why_for_us: Use as a guardrail: persistence after refusal is a risk pattern, not a romance pattern; the slow burn must come from mutual signals.

title: I Did It Because I Never Stopped Loving You: The Effects of Media Portrayals of Persistent Pursuit on Beliefs About Stalking
finding: Experiment: a film depicting persistent pursuit as scary led viewers to endorse fewer stalking-supportive beliefs; a film depicting it as romantic increased such beliefs only among viewers high in perceived realism or transportation (per authors).
why_for_us: Because the series aims at realism, romanticised persistence would hit exactly the most immersed viewers; keep Kuba's pursuit conditional on Zosia's signals.

title: Sexual Harassment Versus Workplace Romance: Social Media Spillover and Textual Harassment in the Workplace
finding: Conceptual/policy article: 'textual harassment' (offensive or inappropriate texts to co-workers) is rising, and social media connectivity blurs the boundary between workplace romance and harassment, requiring new policy thinking (per authors). Not an empirical study.
why_for_us: Late-night texts between two apprentices from related offices must stay clearly welcome and reciprocal; one unanswered flirty message followed by another is the line the show should not cross.
